title: Citric acid and its calcium, potassium and sodium salts
authors: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives
journal: WHO Food Additives Series No. 5, Toxicological evaluation of some food additives including anticaking agents, antimicrobials, antioxidants, emulsifiers and thickening agents; 17th meeting of JECFA, Geneva, 25 June to 4 July 1973; World Health Organization, Geneva
funder: not stated; monograph of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives, published by the World Health Organization.
result: Citric acid is an intermediary substance in oxidative metabolism, engaged in the tricarboxylic acid cycle; citric acid and citrates occur in many foods and are normal metabolites in the body. Ingestion of citric acid frequently or in large doses may cause erosion of teeth and local irritation, apparently because of the low pH; the effects also occur with lemon juice, which contains about 7% citric acid and has a pH below 3. In rats, diets with 1.2% citric acid had no harmful effect on growth or reproduction over two successive generations and 90 weeks, and dental attrition was slightly more marked than in controls; 1380 mg/kg bw per day given orally to three dogs for 112 to 120 days produced no symptoms or renal damage. Citric acid and its calcium, potassium and sodium salts do not constitute a significant toxicological hazard to man; acceptable daily intake not limited.
